Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Massachusetts sued the U.S. government on Wednesday, challenging the constitutionality of a federal law that defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman. The state of Massachusetts says the Defense of Marriage Act denies same-sex couples essential rights. "We're taking this action today because, first, we believe that [the Defense of Marriage Act] directly interferes with Massachusetts' long-standing sovereign authority to define and regulate the marital status of its residents," Attorney General Martha Coakley said Wednesday afternoon. "Massachusetts has a single category of married persons, and we view all married persons equally and identically," she said. "DOMA divides that category into two distinct and unequal classes of marriage." The lawsuit argues that the act, which became law in 1996, denies same-sex couples essential rights and protections, including federal income tax credits, employment and retirement benefits, health insurance coverage and Social Security payments. "In enacting DOMA, Congress overstepped its authority, undermined states' efforts to recognize marriages between same-sex couples, and codified an animus towards gay and lesbian people," the state wrote in the lawsuit, which was filed Wednesday in federal court. Massachusetts, the first state to legalize gay marriage, said that about 16,000 same-sex couples have been married there since 2004, when it began issuing marriage licenses. Since that time, the lawsuit said, "the security and stability of families has been strengthened in important ways throughout the state. " The state is challenging Section 3 of the law, which defines marriage as "a legal union between one man and one woman as husband and wife" and a spouse as "a person of the opposite sex who is a husband or a wife." Before the act, the lawsuit argues, defining marital status was the prerogative of the states. The law "eviscerated more than 200 years of federal government deference to the states with respect to defining marriage," it said. The lawsuit also argues that the law forces Massachusetts to treat same-sex married couples differently from heterosexual married couples, particularly through determining who qualifies for the state's Medicaid program, known as MassHealth, and whether a same-sex spouse of a veteran can be buried in a veteran cemetery. "But for DOMA, married individuals in same-sex relationships in the commonwealth would receive the same status, obligations, responsibilities, rights, and protections as married individuals in different-sex relationships under local, state, and federal laws," the lawsuit said. The defendants named in the lawsuit include the Department of Health and Human Services, Secretary of Health and Human Services Kathleen Sebelius, the Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Affairs Secretary Eric Shinseki and the United States itself. Charles Miller, a spokesman for the Department of Justice, said the department will review the case but noted that President Obama supports the legislative repeal of the Defense of Marriage Act. In March, Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders -- the same Boston-based group that successfully argued in 2003 for same-sex marriage rights in Massachusetts -- also sued the federal government over Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act. Besides Massachusetts, three other states recognize same-sex marriages: Connecticut, Maine, and Iowa. Vermont and New Hampshire will join their company when same-sex marriages become legal later this year and early next year.

State officials contend that the Defense of Marriage Act, known as DOMA, deprives same-sex couples of important legal rights. Speaking Wednesday afternoon, Attorney General Martha Coakley said the state was bringing the case because it believes DOMA “directly interferes” with Massachusetts’ established authority to determine and oversee the marital status of people who live there.

Coakley said Massachusetts recognizes only one class of married people and treats every married person the same. DOMA, she argued, separates that single group into two different and unequal categories of marriage.

According to the lawsuit, the 1996 law withholds key rights and protections from same-sex couples, such as federal income tax credits, workplace and retirement benefits, health insurance coverage, and Social Security payments.

In the complaint filed Wednesday in federal court, Massachusetts said Congress exceeded its power when it passed DOMA, weakened state efforts to acknowledge marriages between same-sex partners, and wrote hostility toward gay and lesbian people into federal law.

Massachusetts was the first state to legalize same-sex marriage. The state said roughly 16,000 same-sex couples have married there since 2004, when it began granting marriage licenses. Since then, the complaint said, families across Massachusetts have gained greater security and stability in significant ways.

The state’s challenge focuses on Section 3 of DOMA. That provision defines marriage as “a legal union between one man and one woman as husband and wife,” and defines a spouse as “a person of the opposite sex who is a husband or a wife.”

The lawsuit argues that, before DOMA was enacted, decisions about marital status belonged to the states. It says the federal law wiped away more than two centuries of federal deference to state governments on the issue of defining marriage.

Massachusetts also claims DOMA requires the state to handle married same-sex couples differently from married heterosexual couples. The state pointed specifically to questions involving eligibility for its Medicaid program, MassHealth, and whether the same-sex spouse of a veteran may be buried in a veterans’ cemetery.

Without DOMA, the lawsuit states, married people in same-sex relationships in Massachusetts would have the same legal status, duties, responsibilities, rights, and protections as married people in different-sex relationships under local, state, and federal law.

The defendants listed in the case include the Department of Health and Human Services; Health and Human Services Secretary Kathleen Sebelius; the Department of Veterans Affairs; Veterans Affairs Secretary Eric Shinseki; and the United States.

Justice Department spokesman Charles Miller said the department would examine the lawsuit. He also noted that President Obama supports repealing the Defense of Marriage Act through legislation.

In March, Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders, the Boston-based organization that successfully argued for same-sex marriage rights in Massachusetts in 2003, also brought a federal lawsuit challenging Section 3 of DOMA.

In addition to Massachusetts, three states recognize same-sex marriage: Connecticut, Maine, and Iowa. Vermont and New Hampshire are set to do the same when same-sex marriage becomes legal there later this year and early next year.

counterfactuals.output:
**Massachusetts AG Martha Coakley Files Constitutional Challenge to DOMA**

**BOSTON —** Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley filed a federal lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the federal Defense of Marriage Act, arguing that the law unlawfully forces Massachusetts to disregard marriages that are valid under state law and deprives married same-sex couples of federal protections and benefits.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Boston, targets Section 3 of DOMA, the 1996 federal law that defines marriage, for all federal purposes, as the union of one man and one woman. Massachusetts, which became the first state to allow same-sex couples to marry in 2004, argues that DOMA intrudes on state authority over marriage and violates constitutional principles of equal treatment and state sovereignty.

“DOMA is a discriminatory law that denies rights and benefits to Massachusetts married couples,” Coakley said in announcing the suit. “The federal government cannot simultaneously recognize that marriage is a matter traditionally left to the states and then refuse to accept lawful marriages performed here.”

Coakley said the case was brought not only on behalf of same-sex couples, but also to protect the Commonwealth’s authority to define and regulate marriage. “Massachusetts has chosen to recognize same-sex marriages,” she said. “DOMA forces the state to treat married couples differently solely because of their sexual orientation, and that is unconstitutional.”

## Legal Arguments

The complaint argues that DOMA Section 3 violates the U.S. Constitution in several ways:

1. **Tenth Amendment / State Sovereignty**  
   Massachusetts contends that marriage has historically been regulated by the states, not the federal government. By refusing to recognize marriages that Massachusetts law deems valid, DOMA allegedly interferes with the state’s sovereign authority.

2. **Spending Clause**  
   The state argues that DOMA places unconstitutional conditions on federal funding by requiring Massachusetts to administer certain federally funded programs in a way that conflicts with state marriage law.

3. **Equal Protection Principles**  
   Although the lawsuit is brought by the Commonwealth, it argues that DOMA creates unequal treatment by denying same-sex married couples the federal recognition automatically provided to different-sex married couples.

4. **Administrative Conflict and Financial Harm**  
   Coakley’s office said DOMA forces Massachusetts agencies to maintain separate systems: one recognizing same-sex marriages under state law and another denying recognition under federal law. The state claims this creates administrative burdens and financial costs.

## Benefits and Programs Affected

The lawsuit identifies several areas where DOMA allegedly harms Massachusetts and its residents:

- **Medicaid / MassHealth:** DOMA can require the state to treat same-sex spouses as legal strangers for federal Medicaid purposes, potentially altering eligibility calculations and shifting costs.

- **Veterans’ Benefits and Burial Rights:** Massachusetts operates state veterans’ cemeteries with federal support. Coakley argues DOMA threatens federal funding if the state allows same-sex spouses of veterans to be buried with the same recognition given to different-sex spouses.

- **Public Employee Benefits:** DOMA affects how health insurance and other benefits for married public employees are treated under federal law.

- **Social Security and Federal Benefits:** Same-sex spouses may be denied survivor benefits, spousal benefits, and other federal protections available to other married couples.

- **Tax Treatment:** Because federal law refuses to recognize same-sex marriages, couples may face different tax consequences even though they are fully married under Massachusetts law.

Coakley’s office said these disparities create a system in which Massachusetts recognizes couples as married while the federal government treats them as unmarried.

## Named Federal Defendants

The lawsuit names several federal agencies and officials responsible for enforcing DOMA in federal programs, including:

- **The United States Department of Health and Human Services**
- **Kathleen Sebelius**, Secretary of Health and Human Services
- **The United States Department of Veterans Affairs**
- **Eric K. Shinseki**, Secretary of Veterans Affairs
- **The United States Office of Personnel Management**
- **John Berry**, Director of the Office of Personnel Management
- **The Social Security Administration**
- **Michael J. Astrue**, Commissioner of Social Security
- **The United States of America**

The suit asks the court to declare Section 3 of DOMA unconstitutional and to prevent federal officials from applying it against Massachusetts and its lawfully married same-sex couples.

## Broader Significance

The case marks the first time a state has directly challenged DOMA in federal court. It comes amid growing national debate over same-sex marriage, with several states recognizing such marriages while the federal government continued to deny recognition under DOMA.

Supporters of the lawsuit argue that DOMA creates a two-tiered marriage system and undermines state authority. Opponents contend that Congress had the power to define marriage for federal purposes and to preserve a uniform federal rule.

Coakley framed the lawsuit as both a civil rights case and a federalism dispute.

“This is about equal treatment under the law,” she said. “But it is also about whether the federal government can disregard decisions made by states in an area that has always belonged to them.”

The case would later become one of the major legal challenges leading toward the U.S. Supreme Court’s eventual review of DOMA.

**Massachusetts Becomes First State to Sue U.S. Government Over DOMA**

BOSTON (AP) — Massachusetts became the first state to challenge the federal Defense of Marriage Act in court Wednesday, arguing that the law interferes with the state’s authority to define marriage and unlawfully denies benefits to married same-sex couples.

Attorney General Martha Coakley filed the lawsuit in federal court in Boston, saying DOMA forces Massachusetts to treat legally married gay and lesbian couples differently from other married couples in areas involving federal programs. The 1996 law defines marriage for federal purposes as the union of one man and one woman and allows states to refuse recognition of same-sex marriages performed elsewhere.

Massachusetts, which became the first state to allow same-sex marriage in 2004, says the federal law has created conflicts in programs the state administers, including MassHealth, the state’s Medicaid program. State officials said DOMA can require Massachusetts to deny or complicate benefits for same-sex spouses even though they are legally married under state law.

The suit also cites veterans’ burial rights, arguing that DOMA prevents the state from providing equal treatment to same-sex spouses seeking burial in state veterans’ cemeteries that receive federal support.

Coakley said the law “forces Massachusetts to engage in a kind of second-class recognition” of marriages the state has chosen to make legal.

The lawsuit comes as President Barack Obama’s administration faces pressure from gay-rights advocates over DOMA. Obama has said he supports repealing the law, but his Justice Department has continued to defend it in court, angering some supporters who say the administration should do more to end federal recognition restrictions on same-sex marriages.

The Massachusetts case is separate from a lawsuit filed earlier this year by Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders, or GLAD, on behalf of same-sex couples and surviving spouses who say DOMA has denied them federal benefits, including Social Security, tax and retirement protections.

Several states have joined Massachusetts in recognizing same-sex marriage. Connecticut and Iowa allow gay and lesbian couples to marry, while Vermont has approved same-sex marriage, with the law set to take effect later this year. New Hampshire and Maine also enacted marriage laws in 2009, though Maine’s law faced a possible voter referendum.

Supporters of DOMA say the federal government has the right to set its own definition of marriage for federal benefits and that states should not be forced to recognize marriages that conflict with their laws.

The Massachusetts lawsuit asks the court to declare the federal definition of marriage unconstitutional as applied to couples legally married under state law.
